questions.stem: You are leading the move of a building society's core systems to a new data centre. The client has moved the cutover from a Wednesday night to the following Saturday because a mid-week cutover would clash with its quarter-end payment run. Your infrastructure team has heard only that the date changed, and several engineers are openly annoyed about losing a weekend. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Agree time off in lieu for everyone working on the Saturday and publish the revised rota, so the practical impact of the change is settled quickly.
options.rationale: Compensation is fair and probably needed, but it answers the cost and not the complaint. A candidate choosing this assumes the grievance is about hours, when the team does not yet know why its weekend was taken.

options.text: Ask the client whether the cutover could return to the weekday if the team added extra rehearsals to reduce the risk to the payment run.
options.rationale: This reopens a client decision taken for a sound business reason in order to relieve internal grumbling. It treats the team's mood as a reason to renegotiate rather than something the project manager can address directly.

options.text: Tell the team the date is the client's decision and outside the project's control, and ask the leads to manage any concerns within their own areas.
options.rationale: True, but it passes on the decision without its reason and hands the leads a problem they have no more information to solve. Saying a decision is someone else's is not the same as explaining it.

options.text: Brief the team on why the client moved the cutover, including the quarter-end payment clash, before agreeing the weekend rota with them.
options.rationale: The annoyance is about a decision that looks arbitrary from where the team sits. Giving them the reason turns an imposed inconvenience into a trade-off they can understand, and the rota conversation then starts from shared facts.

questions.explanation: People accept inconvenient decisions far more readily when they know the reason behind them; a team given only the outcome fills the gap with its own explanation, usually an unflattering one. Passing on the why is cheap, fast and within any leader's power, and it should come before discussions about compensation or arrangements, because those conversations go better when everyone agrees the decision was reasonable.
questions.mindset: Pass on the reason with the decision, because a decision without its reason invites the team to supply one.

questions.stem: Your team builds a payments app for a fintech start-up. Velocity has risen from 34 to 46 points over three sprints, and the product owner has praised the improvement at every review. Looking at the repository, you notice that four developers have been committing code on Saturdays and Sundays throughout that period. Nobody has mentioned weekend work at standups or in the last retrospective. What should you do?

options.text: Raise the weekend commits openly at the next retrospective, so the team can look at what the recent velocity has cost and decide what pace to plan for.
options.rationale: The velocity figure is currently misleading everyone, the product owner included, because it hides the hours behind it. Putting the evidence in front of the team lets them own the decision about sustainable pace rather than having it made for them.

options.text: Ask the product owner to stop praising the velocity increase at sprint reviews, so the developers do not feel pressure to keep the figures rising.
options.rationale: This guesses at the cause and treats one possible symptom. The candidate assumes the praise is driving the hours, but nobody has yet asked the team why the weekend work is happening or whether they see it as a problem.

options.text: Speak privately to each of the four developers, ask them to stop working at weekends, and to log any overtime they believe is necessary so that it shows in the team's capacity figures.
options.rationale: It handles a team-level planning issue as four individual conduct issues. The forecast the whole team commits to is built on hidden hours, and only the team together can decide to plan differently.

options.text: Reduce the next sprint's forecast to the earlier average of 34 points, so the developers have no reason to work beyond their normal hours.
options.rationale: The forecast belongs to the developers, and setting it for them removes ownership they will need to protect their own pace. The candidate also assumes the hours are caused by the forecast rather than finding out.

questions.explanation: A performance measure that is propped up by unreported effort misleads everyone who plans with it, and the longer it runs the more the inflated figure becomes the expectation. The leader's job is to bring the hidden cost into the open in a forum the team owns, so the team can decide on a pace it can sustain. Unilateral fixes, private or public, take that decision away from the people who have to live with it.
questions.mindset: When a number improves suddenly, find out what it cost before you celebrate it.

questions.stem: You lead a pharmaceutical team preparing a regulatory submission. Six weeks ago you told the team the filing deadline was 14 March, and every work package has been planned to that date. This morning, rereading the regulator's guidance, you realise you misread it: the deadline is 28 February. Nobody else has spotted the error, and the team is working to the original plan. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Draft a revised schedule overnight that recovers the two weeks, and present it to the team tomorrow together with the corrected deadline.
options.rationale: It looks responsible, but it delays the correction by a day while the team keeps working to a wrong date, and it presents them with a finished plan they had no part in. The candidate is trying to arrive with the fix and the error together.

options.text: Ask the regulatory affairs lead whether an extension to 14 March could be requested, before telling the team anything about the error.
options.rationale: It makes disclosure conditional on whether the mistake can be made to disappear. Even if an extension is possible, the team is planning on false information today, and a leader seen to manage around their own error loses credibility.

options.text: Tell the sponsor about the error and the schedule risk first, and agree with them how and when to announce the corrected date to the team.
options.rationale: The sponsor does need to know, but not as a gate in front of the team. The candidate is treating the correction as a governance message, when the people acting on the wrong date every hour are the team.

options.text: Tell the team today that you misread the deadline, then re-plan the remaining work packages with them against the correct date.
options.rationale: Every hour of delay is an hour of work planned to the wrong date. Owning the mistake openly and immediately also models the behaviour the leader wants from the team when they get something wrong.

questions.explanation: When a leader discovers that the team is acting on wrong information the leader gave them, the correction is urgent and personal: delay compounds the damage, and how the leader owns the mistake sets the standard for how the team will handle its own. Informing governance and seeking mitigation are both legitimate, but neither should stand between the team and the facts they are working from.
questions.mindset: Own your own mistakes as quickly and openly as you would want the team to own theirs.

questions.stem: On an online retailer's checkout team, the commercial director has started messaging two developers directly with small changes to the checkout page. Keen to help, they have been fitting the changes in between sprint items, and the sprint goal is now at risk with four days left. The product owner is not aware of the requests. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Tell the two developers to decline any request that does not come through the product owner, and to refer the director politely to the product backlog and its refinement sessions.
options.rationale: The rule is right but the person enforcing it is wrong. Asking two developers to turn down a director puts them in an uncomfortable position the leader should be absorbing on their behalf.

options.text: Reserve a fixed amount of capacity in each sprint for the director's requests, so the developers can keep helping without the sprint goal being put at risk.
options.rationale: It legitimises the bypass and takes ordering decisions away from the product owner for a slice of every sprint. The candidate is solving the capacity symptom rather than the routing problem.

options.text: Raise the pattern at the sprint review in front of the stakeholders, so the director sees the effect of the requests on the delivered increment.
options.rationale: It waits until the damage is done and then makes the point in public, which is likely to embarrass the director rather than change the route. A private conversation now achieves more at lower cost.

options.text: Speak with the commercial director, explain the effect on the sprint goal, and agree that requests go to the product owner, who can prioritise them quickly.
options.rationale: The director has a legitimate need and has found the wrong route to it. Redirecting the requests to the product owner protects the team's focus while giving the director a route that still works for them.

questions.explanation: Part of leading a team is absorbing the pressure that would otherwise land on individual members, particularly from people senior to them. When a stakeholder goes around the agreed route, the leader redirects the stakeholder to the person who owns the decision, rather than asking team members to refuse, building the bypass into the plan, or making an example of anyone.
questions.mindset: Stand between the team and the pressure, and send each request to whoever owns the decision.

questions.stem: You manage a water utility's mains-replacement programme. At the steering meeting, the sponsor thanks you personally for re-sequencing the valve replacements around school holidays, which has cut disruption complaints by a third. The idea came from Amira, a junior planner on your team, who is not at the meeting. The sponsor's thanks will be recorded in the minutes. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Accept the thanks on behalf of the team, and recognise Amira's contribution at the next team meeting where her colleagues can hear it.
options.rationale: Recognising her in front of peers is good, but the record that reaches the sponsor still credits the wrong person. The candidate is treating team-level credit as enough, when the most valuable audience for her idea is the one in the room now.

options.text: Say in the meeting that the re-sequencing was Amira's idea, and pass the sponsor's comments on to her directly afterwards.
options.rationale: The moment to correct the record is while it is being made. Naming her in front of the sponsor costs nothing and puts her work in front of the people who influence her career.

options.text: Ask the sponsor after the meeting to send Amira a note of thanks, so the recognition comes from someone more senior than you.
options.rationale: A note from the sponsor is worth having, but the minutes will already say the idea was yours. The candidate is postponing the correction to a moment when it is less visible and depends on someone else.

options.text: Nominate Amira for the company's quarterly recognition award, citing the fall in complaints as evidence of the impact her idea has had.
options.rationale: A fine follow-up, but it does nothing about the credit being recorded today. A candidate choosing it is looking for the biggest gesture rather than the most immediate one.

questions.explanation: Credit that is misattributed in a senior forum is hard to correct later, because the record and the impression have already formed. A leader who redirects credit to its source in the moment builds trust that later gestures cannot buy, and shows the team that good ideas will be seen by the people who matter whoever has them.
questions.mindset: Give credit where the work came from, at the moment the credit is being given.

questions.stem: Your team builds route-planning software for a logistics firm. For two weeks the developers have debated which of two message-queue libraries to adopt. They have written up a comparison showing both meet every requirement, and switching later would take about two days. The disagreement is now holding up three stories. At the end of a long discussion, the team asks you, as delivery lead, to make the call. What should you do?

options.text: Ask the team to run a time-boxed spike using both libraries, so the decision rests on evidence from their own code rather than on opinion.
options.rationale: A spike reduces uncertainty, but the team has already established that both options work and that the choice is cheap to undo. The candidate is buying more information for a decision whose cost of delay is now higher than its cost of being wrong.

options.text: Facilitate a structured vote, such as fist of five, so the team reaches its own decision and keeps ownership of the technical choice.
options.rationale: Facilitation is often the right instinct, but this team has already spent two weeks failing to reach a decision and has asked for one. The candidate is applying a self-organisation principle past the point where it serves the team.

options.text: Make the decision now, explain your reasoning to the team, and note that it can be revisited if new evidence comes to light later.
options.rationale: The team has done the analysis, failed to converge and explicitly asked for a decision. For a cheap, reversible choice that is blocking work, a prompt decision with stated reasoning is the most useful thing the leader can give.

options.text: Refer the choice to the enterprise architecture group, which has a wider view of the libraries already in use across the organisation.
options.rationale: Nothing in the scenario suggests an organisational standard is at stake. Sending a two-day, reversible choice to another group adds delay and moves the decision away from anyone close to the work.

questions.explanation: Empowering a team does not mean refusing to decide when the team asks for a decision. Match the effort spent on a decision to its cost of reversal: a cheap, reversible choice that is blocking work deserves a quick call with the reasoning shown, while an expensive, hard-to-undo one deserves more analysis and wider ownership. Withholding a decision the team has requested can itself become an impediment.
questions.mindset: Spend decision effort in proportion to how hard the decision is to undo.

questions.stem: On a highway-widening project, Sinead, a senior surveyor, tells you privately that her father has been diagnosed with a serious illness. She wants to keep working but expects to need absences at short notice over the next two months. She is currently assigned the topographic survey of a bridge approach, which sits on the critical path and is due in five weeks. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Agree flexible working with her, and re-plan her assignments together so the time-critical bridge fieldwork no longer depends on her availability.
options.rationale: It honours her decision to keep working and her privacy, while removing the conflict between her circumstances and the critical path. Re-planning with her keeps her in control of how her situation is handled.

options.text: Keep her on the bridge survey as she prefers, and assign a back-up surveyor to shadow her so that cover is ready if she is called away.
options.rationale: It respects her wish but leaves the critical path dependent on someone who has said she may be unavailable at short notice, and doubles the resource to do it. The candidate is accommodating her without adapting the plan.

options.text: Suggest she takes a period of compassionate leave so she can focus on her family, and reassign the bridge survey and her other work until she feels ready to return.
options.rationale: Kindly meant, but it overrides what she has just told you she wants. The candidate assumes they know better than she does what she needs, which is the opposite of the trust she showed in telling you.

options.text: Explain the situation to the team so they understand why she may be absent at short notice, and ask for volunteers to cover her work.
options.rationale: She told you privately, and sharing it without her consent breaches that confidence however supportive the motive. The candidate is solving the cover problem with information that was not theirs to share.

questions.explanation: When a team member's circumstances change, the leader's task is to adapt the work around the person rather than force a choice between their life and the plan. That means taking their stated wishes at face value, keeping personal information within the bounds they set, and moving time-critical work away from known availability risks with their involvement.
questions.mindset: Adapt the plan to the person, and let them decide how much of their situation others need to know.

questions.stem: For a museum exhibition fit-out, you delegated authority to the build team to choose audio-visual suppliers up to €40,000. They chose a smaller supplier offering a better specification at a lower price than the museum's usual vendor. That supplier is now three weeks late and the opening date is at risk. The museum director asks you whether the team should still be choosing suppliers. How should the project manager respond?

options.text: Keep the delegation in place and back the team publicly, because the decision sat within their limit and was reasonable on both price and specification at the time it was made.
options.rationale: Backing the team is often right, but this asserts the decision was sound before anyone has checked. The candidate is defending the delegation on principle when the question deserves an answer based on what the team knew.

options.text: Take supplier selection back for the rest of the project, and restore the team's authority on the next project once the opening is secured.
options.rationale: It judges the delegation on one bad outcome and teaches the team that authority lasts only until something goes wrong. The candidate is reacting to the result without knowing whether the decision itself was poor.

options.text: Tell the director you will first review the selection with the team, to see whether the delay was foreseeable from what they knew, before changing the delegation.
options.rationale: A bad outcome can come from a bad decision or from bad luck, and the right response to each is different. Reviewing the decision against the information available at the time gives the director a real answer and protects the delegation from an unexamined verdict.

options.text: Add a requirement that the team checks delivery track record for any supplier over €10,000, and keep the rest of the delegation unchanged.
options.rationale: A sensible-looking control, but it assumes the cause is a missing track-record check before anyone has established that. The candidate is fixing a guessed cause, which may leave the real one untouched.

questions.explanation: A delegated decision should be judged by the quality of the decision given what was known at the time, not by its outcome alone. Before tightening, withdrawing or defending delegated authority, establish whether the failure was foreseeable: if it was, the decision process needs changing; if it was not, withdrawing authority punishes reasonable judgement and teaches the team to avoid decisions. Either way the diagnosis comes before the change.
questions.mindset: Separate a bad decision from a bad outcome before deciding what a failure says about the people who made it.

questions.stem: Your game studio team has five developers in Lisbon and two in Auckland, which is thirteen hours ahead. The daily sync runs at 09:00 Lisbon time, 22:00 in Auckland, and there is no hour that falls inside normal working time in both cities. The Auckland pair have not complained, but they have started joining with cameras off and rarely speak. What should you do?

options.text: Keep the 09:00 slot because the Auckland developers have not objected, and check in each of their one-to-ones whether the late finish is sustainable for them over a longer period.
options.rationale: It waits for a complaint that the two people with least standing in the arrangement may not make. The candidate is reading silence as consent when the behaviour change is already a signal.

options.text: Agree with the whole team a schedule that shares the inconvenience, for example alternating the sync so Lisbon also takes some evening sessions.
options.rationale: With no shared working hour, someone has to be inconvenienced, and the fair answer is that it is not always the same people. Agreeing it with the whole team makes the cost visible and shared.

options.text: Let the Auckland pair contribute by written update instead of attending, so they keep normal hours while the Lisbon developers meet as usual.
options.rationale: It solves their hours by turning them into a second tier of the team who are reported to rather than included. The candidate trades their evenings for their participation.

options.text: Move the sync to 08:00 in Lisbon, which is 21:00 in Auckland, so both locations give up a little of their normal day for the meeting.
options.rationale: It looks like a compromise but the cost still falls almost entirely on Auckland: an hour earlier for Lisbon against a late evening every day for Auckland. The candidate mistakes a small adjustment for a shared burden.

questions.explanation: In a distributed team with no overlapping working hours, the cost of meeting together has to fall on someone, and leaving it on the minority location by default quietly signals whose time matters. The fair approach is to make the trade-off explicit and agree with the whole team how the inconvenience is shared, rather than waiting for the people bearing it to object.
questions.mindset: When someone has to bear a cost for the team, make sure it is not always the same people.

questions.stem: You lead a council's housing-repairs system replacement. At a closed steering meeting you learn that the project may be paused at its gate review in six weeks because of budget pressure, and the sponsor asks you to keep this confidential until the board decides. The next day two team leads ask you directly whether the rumours that the project is being cancelled are true. What should the project manager say?

options.text: Say you cannot share steering discussions, that the project faces its normal gate review in six weeks, and that you will brief them as soon as you can.
options.rationale: It keeps the confidence without creating a false impression, and gives the leads what they can rely on: the review is real, and they will hear when there is news. Honesty about what you cannot say is still honesty.

options.text: Point out that the project is meeting all of its current milestones, and ask them to keep their teams focused on delivery rather than on rumours they cannot verify.
options.rationale: Nothing said is false, but it is chosen to leave them believing there is nothing to the rumours. A candidate choosing it is protecting the confidence by misleading, which costs far more trust when the decision becomes known.

options.text: Ask the sponsor for permission to share the possibility with the two leads in confidence, as they need it for their own team planning.
options.rationale: It asks the sponsor to widen a confidence they set deliberately, for a need the leads do not yet have, since their current work is unchanged. The leads still need an honest answer today.

options.text: Share the possibility with the two leads in confidence, since they are senior enough to handle it and are likely to hear the rumours anyway.
options.rationale: It breaks a commitment made the day before, on the leader's own judgement that the people asking are trustworthy. The candidate is trading the sponsor's trust for the team's.

questions.explanation: A leader holding confidential information has two obligations that can feel in conflict: keep the confidence, and do not mislead the team. Both can be met by saying plainly that there are things you cannot share, confirming what is genuinely known, and committing to tell them when you can. Reassurance that implies a false picture breaks the second obligation as surely as disclosure breaks the first.
questions.mindset: You can decline to say something without saying something untrue.

questions.stem: You lead a hybrid programme replacing a university's student records system: a fixed data-migration plan alongside two agile squads. The sponsor, worried about pace, asks you to publish a weekly table showing how many tickets each developer closed, so that low performers can be identified. The squads pair-program on most stories and work as one team on defects. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Produce the table for the sponsor only, without publishing it to the team, so the information is available without affecting how people work together.
options.rationale: Keeping it private limits the damage to morale but not the damage to the decision. A per-person count of paired work will still mislead the sponsor about who is contributing, and the team will hear of it.

options.text: Weight each closed ticket by its story-point size before publishing, so the table reflects the difficulty of the work rather than the raw count of tickets.
options.rationale: Weighting improves the arithmetic but keeps the flawed premise: in a pairing team, who closed a ticket says little about who did the work. The candidate is refining a measure that should be questioned.

options.text: Explain to the sponsor why per-person counts would mislead and distort behaviour here, and offer team-level delivery measures plus a route for raising any specific performance concern.
options.rationale: The sponsor's real concern is pace and possible underperformance, both legitimate. Addressing that concern with measures that fit collaborative work, and a direct route for individual issues, meets the need without introducing a measure that would push people to stop helping one another.

options.text: Ask both squads at their next retrospectives whether they would accept a per-person table and how it would change their work, and go back to the sponsor with the team's view before agreeing to anything.
options.rationale: Consulting the team respects them, but it hands them a governance question the leader should answer and frames it as a matter of comfort rather than validity. The leader already has the knowledge to advise the sponsor.

questions.explanation: Individual output counts in work that is done collaboratively both mismeasure contribution and change behaviour, since people stop pairing, reviewing and picking up defects that do not score. When a senior stakeholder asks for such a measure, the leader's role is to engage with the concern behind the request and offer measures that answer it, rather than comply, soften the measure, or pass the decision to the team.
questions.mindset: Answer the concern behind a request, not just the request, when the request would damage the team.

questions.stem: At a medical-device maker, hardware follows a stage-gated plan while firmware is built in sprints. Joanna, a capable mid-level firmware engineer, asks to lead hardware–firmware integration for the next release. She has never led integration, and the release has a fixed regulatory submission date. Your most experienced engineer, Viktor, has led the last four integrations and is willing to do it again. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask Joanna to lead integration on a smaller internal release first, and give her the regulated release once she has shown she can handle the role.
options.rationale: A cautious, common approach, but it delays her development to a release that may not come soon and treats one lower-stakes run as a prerequisite the plan does not need. The candidate is avoiding the trade-off rather than managing it.

options.text: Give Joanna the integration lead with agreed checkpoints before each gate, and ask Viktor to act as her adviser rather than as the lead.
options.rationale: It accepts a managed amount of risk in exchange for building a second integration lead, and puts the experience the team has in a supporting role where it can catch problems early. The checkpoints keep the submission date protected.

options.text: Keep Viktor as integration lead for this release and have Joanna work alongside him throughout, so she is fully prepared to lead the following one.
options.rationale: Shadowing is safer, but it leaves the team dependent on one person for another full cycle and gives Joanna observation rather than responsibility. The candidate is weighting short-term certainty over the capability the team needs.

options.text: Give Joanna the integration lead and let her decide when to check in with you, so she has full ownership and the confidence that comes with it.
options.rationale: Ownership matters, but a first-time lead on a release with a fixed regulatory date needs agreed points at which problems surface. The candidate equates empowerment with stepping away entirely.

questions.explanation: Developing people means giving them real responsibility before they are fully proven, and that always carries some risk. The leader's task is to size and contain the risk, through checkpoints, access to experienced support and a clear route for escalation, rather than avoid it by deferring the opportunity or remove all structure in the name of trust.
questions.mindset: Grow people by giving them real responsibility with a safety net, not by waiting until no risk remains.

questions.stem: Your team at an insurance comparison site can finish a change in two days, but every release must pass the security change board, which meets fortnightly. Over the last quarter finished work waited an average of nine days for approval, and the developers have started batching changes into larger releases to reduce the number of submissions. As delivery lead, which two actions should you take?

options.text: Collect the waiting-time data for the last quarter and present it to the board's chair, showing what the delay is costing in lead time and in release size.
options.rationale: The board probably does not see the delay its schedule creates or the larger, riskier releases it is encouraging. Evidence presented to the person who owns the process is the starting point for changing it.

options.text: Propose to the security team a lighter, pre-agreed approval route for low-risk changes, with the full board reserved for changes that need it.
options.rationale: It meets the board's purpose, controlling security risk, while removing the wait for changes that carry little of it. Offering a workable alternative makes the request easier to agree to.

options.text: Encourage the developers to keep batching changes, since fewer submissions mean less total time lost to the board's fortnightly cycle.
options.rationale: Batching adapts to the impediment instead of removing it, and makes each release larger and riskier, which is exactly what a security review is meant to reduce. The candidate is optimising around the problem.

options.text: Add the expected nine-day approval wait to the team's forecasts, so stakeholders see realistic delivery dates and are not disappointed by delays.
options.rationale: Honest forecasting is good, but on its own it treats the wait as a fixed fact of life. The candidate is managing expectations about the impediment rather than working to remove it.

options.text: Ask the CIO to instruct the security board to meet weekly, since the delay is affecting delivery across the team's whole portfolio of work.
options.rationale: Going over the board's head before talking to it is likely to harden positions, and a weekly meeting still leaves several days of waiting. The candidate is escalating before using the influence they have.

questions.explanation: Organisational processes that slow a team are impediments the team usually cannot remove on its own, and they fall to the leader. The effective route is to make the cost visible to whoever owns the process and offer an alternative that still serves its purpose; working around the impediment, absorbing it into forecasts or escalating over the owner's head leaves it in place or sours the relationship needed to change it.
questions.mindset: Treat a slow process as an impediment to remove with its owner, not a fact to plan around.

questions.stem: You are managing a planned maintenance shutdown of a chemical plant, with forty fitters working in shifts. Site rules give every worker authority to stop a job they believe is unsafe. In six weeks nobody has used it, although two fitters later admitted carrying on with tasks they were uneasy about. The only stop called so far led to the fitter being questioned for an hour at the project's own incident review. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Tell every shift at its briefing that you will back any stop called in good faith, and attend the next stop-work review yourself to make sure that happens.
options.rationale: The fitters have watched what happened to the last person who used the authority, so a personal commitment from the person who runs the project, followed by being seen to keep it, is what changes their reading of the risk.

options.text: Change the project's incident review so that a stop is examined for the unsafe condition and its fix, rather than for the decision of the person who called it.
options.rationale: The review is the project's own process and it is the thing deterring people. Changing what it examines removes the penalty at its source, which is within the project manager's authority to do today.

options.text: Run a refresher session on the stop-work procedure for every shift, so that each fitter knows exactly when and how to use the authority the site gives them.
options.rationale: It assumes the fitters do not know the procedure, when the two admissions show they knew and chose not to use it. The candidate is treating a consequence problem as a knowledge problem.

options.text: Add the number of stop-work calls per shift to the weekly safety report, so that supervisors have a reason to encourage their crews to use the authority.
options.rationale: A count invites supervisors to manage the number rather than the fear behind it, and does nothing about the review that put people off. The candidate is reaching for a measure before removing the deterrent.

options.text: Ask the client's safety director to write to all contractors on site confirming that stop-work authority will be respected and that nobody will be penalised for using it.
options.rationale: A letter from elsewhere is weaker than a change the project manager can make directly, because the deterrent sits in the project's own review. The candidate is routing upward a problem they already own.

questions.explanation: Authority granted on paper is used only when people have seen that using it is safe. When a team leaves an authority unused, look first at what happened the last time someone used it, then remove that consequence in the parts of the system the leader controls and be visibly behind the next person who acts. Training, targets and statements issued by others leave the deterrent where it is.
questions.mindset: People use the authority you give them only after they have seen it is safe to use.

questions.stem: Your team spent nine months building a claims self-service portal for an insurer. Two weeks before launch, the board shelved it after deciding to partner with an external claims platform instead, and your team has been moved to integrate with that platform. Morale has dropped, and one engineer said at standup that nothing they build seems to matter. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Explain the board's reasons for the decision openly, and acknowledge to the team what the portal work cost them and what it achieved.
options.rationale: The team needs to know the decision was a business judgement rather than a verdict on their work. Acknowledging the loss is what lets them put it down rather than carry it into the next piece of work.

options.text: Start the integration work immediately, so the team builds momentum on the new goal rather than dwelling on the shelved portal.
options.rationale: Momentum helps, but moving on without addressing the engineer's comment leaves the belief that their work does not matter in place. The candidate is treating a motivation problem as a scheduling one.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to release the portal as a limited pilot for a small customer group, so that the team's work reaches real users.
options.rationale: It tries to undo a business decision to soothe the team, putting the sponsor in an awkward position and possibly creating a product nobody will maintain. The candidate is resisting the change rather than adapting to it.

options.text: Identify with the team what from the portal can be reused in the integration, and involve them in shaping how the new work is approached.
options.rationale: It connects nine months of effort to the new goal and gives the team influence over what comes next, which addresses the sense that their work counts for nothing.

options.text: Arrange a team event to celebrate completing the portal, so the effort is marked properly before the team moves on to the integration.
options.rationale: Marking the effort is a kind gesture, but a celebration of a product that will not launch may feel hollow without the reasons and the link to what comes next. The candidate is offering recognition in place of meaning.

questions.explanation: When a team's work is cancelled for reasons outside its control, motivation depends less on consolation than on understanding why it happened and seeing that its effort carries into what comes next. A leader explains the decision honestly, acknowledges the loss, and connects the team to the new goal with a say in how it is pursued, rather than fighting the decision or skipping straight past it.
questions.mindset: When work is cancelled, give the team the reasons and a stake in what comes next.

questions.stem: You are agile delivery lead for a team building a box-office app for a theatre group. Match each obstacle raised at the daily standup to the response that fits it best. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: The test suite fails intermittently because of an unreliable test that two of the developers wrote themselves last month.
The payment provider has ignored the team's requests for sandbox access for nine days, and the contract with it is held by the finance department.
A developer finds that the story she picked is twice the size estimated, and the sprint goal depends on part of it.

options.text: Leave it with the team to fix, and ask at the next standup how they got on
options.rationale: The problem is inside the team's own code and skills, so the team is the fastest route to removing it. Taking it over would teach them to hand up problems they can solve themselves.

options.text: Take it on yourself and chase it through the contract owner in finance
options.rationale: The team has no lever over an external supplier whose contract sits with another department. Reaching outside the team on its behalf is exactly the obstacle a servant leader exists to clear.

options.text: Bring the developer and the product owner together to agree which part to deliver this sprint
options.rationale: Deciding what to drop or keep is a value decision, and value belongs to the product owner. Bringing the two together lets the scope be cut deliberately rather than by default at the end of the sprint.

options.text: Log it on the impediment board and raise it at the sprint retrospective
options.rationale: Not used. Every one of these is blocking work now, and the retrospective is for improving how the team works rather than for clearing today's blockers. Logging an obstacle is not the same as getting it removed.

questions.explanation: An obstacle should go to whoever can remove it soonest. Problems inside the team's own control stay with the team, because solving them builds its capability; obstacles that need reach outside the team are the leader's to clear; and obstacles that are really choices about scope or value go to the person who owns those choices. Holding obstacles for a later review leaves them blocking the work in the meantime.
questions.mindset: Send each obstacle to whoever can remove it soonest, and keep with the team the ones it can solve itself.

questions.stem: You manage the construction of a rail depot. Match each situation on site to the way the project manager should handle the feedback it calls for. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: A technician's careful isolation check before maintenance work prevented what could have been a serious electrical incident.
A site supervisor has submitted the crew's timesheets late for four weeks running, delaying the subcontractors' payments.
A whole crew installed drainage to the wrong levels because the method statement they were given was ambiguous.

options.text: Recognise it publicly at the next toolbox talk
options.rationale: Public recognition rewards the person and shows everyone on site which behaviour matters. On a safety-critical site it also reinforces the habit you most want others to copy.

options.text: Raise it in a private conversation with the individual
options.rationale: Corrective feedback about one person's performance belongs in private, where they can explain and agree a fix without losing face in front of their crew.

options.text: Review the method statement with the crew, without assigning individual blame
options.rationale: The cause is the instruction rather than the people following it. Reviewing it with the crew fixes the source of the error and keeps them willing to report the next one.

options.text: Issue a formal written warning through human resources
options.rationale: Not used. Formal discipline is for serious or persistent misconduct after informal routes have failed. None of these situations has reached that point, and one of them deserves praise.

questions.explanation: Feedback works when its setting fits its purpose: praise in public, where it reinforces the behaviour for everyone; correct an individual in private, where they can respond without losing face; and treat errors caused by a system or an instruction as a matter for the group, without blame. Getting the setting wrong can turn praise into embarrassment or correction into humiliation.
questions.mindset: Praise in public, correct in private, and fix the system when the system caused the error.

questions.stem: You lead a programme at an energy retailer that is introducing a release process combining stage gates with sprints. You have noticed that influence in the team does not follow job titles. Complete each sentence with the response that fits. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: In estimation sessions the team waits for the senior tester's figure and then settles on it, even when their own view differs. You should
A well-liked developer is openly sceptical of the new release process in informal conversations, and colleagues are starting to repeat her doubts. You should
A contractor with deep knowledge of the billing system is rarely listened to in design discussions because he is new and not a permanent employee. You should

options.text: have everyone reveal their estimates at the same moment, before any discussion starts
options.rationale: The problem is anchoring on one respected voice, not the tester's behaviour. Revealing estimates together gets each person's own view on the table before influence can act on it, without silencing anyone.

options.text: involve her in refining the process and treat her objections as design input
options.rationale: Her influence will shape how the team receives the process either way. Bringing her into the design turns a credible critic into someone with a stake in making it work, and her objections may well be right.

options.text: ask him to lead the next design walkthrough on the billing interfaces
options.rationale: His expertise is being discounted because of his status, so the remedy is to give it a visible platform where the team can see what he knows. Status follows demonstrated knowledge quickly once it has a stage.

options.text: raise the pattern openly at the next retrospective and ask the team to discuss it
options.rationale: Not used. Each pattern centres on one named person, and discussing it in a group forum puts that person on the spot. In each case the leader can change the dynamic directly by changing how the work is run.

questions.explanation: Informal influence follows credibility, popularity and status rather than the organisation chart, and a leader works with it rather than against it. Where one voice anchors the group, change the process so independent views appear first; where an influential sceptic is shaping opinion, involve them in the design; where real expertise is ignored because of status, give it a visible platform. Suppressing influence or putting it on trial in public tends to drive it underground.
questions.mindset: Map where influence actually sits in the team, then design the work so it helps rather than distorts.

questions.stem: Your seven-engineer team at a broadcaster has a 10-working-day phase ahead. Two engineers each have 2 days of booked leave. Each engineer delivers 6 productive hours a day, and 10% of the team's productive hours are reserved for the support rota. The phase plan you inherited commits 450 hours of work. Work out the hours actually available and how far the plan exceeds them.

blanks.label: Hours available for planned work in the phase
blanks.rationale: Engineer-days are 7 × 10 = 70, less 2 × 2 = 4 days of leave, giving 66. At 6 productive hours that is 396 hours, and reserving 10% for support leaves 396 × 0.9 = 356.4 hours.

blanks.label: Amount by which the plan exceeds available hours, as a percentage
blanks.rationale: 450 ÷ 356.4 = 1.263, so the plan asks for about 26% more than the team can deliver at a sustainable pace. That gap will be met by overtime, cut corners or a missed phase end unless it is raised now.

questions.explanation: A plan that commits more than the team's real capacity does not make the team faster; it moves the shortfall into overtime, quality or slipped dates, usually without anyone deciding that it should. Real capacity accounts for leave, productive hours and work the team must do anyway, and the leader's job is to show the gap in figures before the work starts, so that scope or dates can be adjusted deliberately.
questions.mindset: Show the gap between the plan and the team's real capacity before the team pays for it.

questions.stem: The diagram is your team's skills matrix, one row per skill, showing current expertise and the sprint in which the skill is next needed. Next sprint is sprint 14. Select the skill that presents the most urgent key-person risk and should be the first target for cross-training.

graphic.title: Team skills matrix with expert count, trainees and next sprint each skill is needed
graphic.caption: Select a skill row. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between rows, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Front-end development — 3 experts, 1 in training, needed sprint 14
regions.rationale: Three experts already cover this skill, so losing any one of them would not stop the work. Adding a fourth trainee here spends effort where the risk is lowest.

regions.label: Database migration — 1 expert (Priya), 0 in training, needed sprint 14
regions.rationale: One person holds the skill, nobody is learning it, and it is needed next sprint. Any absence would stop that work immediately, so this is the gap to start closing first.

regions.label: Test automation — 1 expert, 2 in training, needed sprint 14
regions.rationale: Only one expert, but two people are already learning it and can carry some of the load. The risk is real but already being reduced.

regions.label: Accessibility testing — 0 experts, 0 in training, needed sprint 22
regions.rationale: This is a capability gap rather than a key-person risk, and it is eight sprints away. It needs planning, but choosing it first confuses the larger gap with the more urgent one.

regions.label: Release management — 2 experts, 0 in training, needed sprint 15
regions.rationale: Two experts give cover if one is away, so this skill is not dependent on a single person. It is worth watching, but it is not the most urgent.

questions.explanation: Key-person risk is greatest where a skill is held by one person, nobody else is learning it, and the work that needs it is close. Reading a skills matrix means weighing all three together: a wider gap that is further away can wait for planning, while a single holder of a skill needed next sprint calls for cross-training now. Building redundancy into the team is part of leading it, not a separate exercise.
questions.mindset: Look for where the team depends on one person for work that is coming soon.

questions.stem: You manage the construction of a secondary school extension. Site rules require hard hats and high-visibility vests beyond the site office. At this morning's briefing a foreman tells you, politely, that operatives have noticed you walking the site without either on short visits, and some have started doing the same on quick errands. You had assumed brief walk-throughs did not matter. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Wear the full kit on every visit from now on, and leave it at that so the lapse is not given more attention than it deserves.
options.rationale: Quietly correcting your own behaviour fixes the next visit but not the lesson the crew has already drawn, which is that the rule bends for seniors. A lapse that was seen needs to be owned where it was seen, or the copied habit carries on.

options.text: Ask the site manager to reissue the PPE rule to all personnel, managers included, with a reminder that it applies to short visits too.
options.rationale: This treats your own example as a communication gap. A general reminder lets the source of the habit go unmentioned, and the crew will read it as the rule being restated at them rather than the manager taking responsibility.

options.text: Thank the foreman, start wearing the kit yourself, and ask the supervisors to challenge any operative they see without it on quick errands.
options.rationale: It puts the enforcement burden on operatives for a habit they learned from you, while your own part is never acknowledged. Tightening supervision without owning the cause tends to breed resentment rather than compliance.

options.text: Acknowledge the lapse at the next crew briefing, thank the foreman for raising it, and wear the full kit on every visit from now on.
options.rationale: The crew copied what they saw, so they need to see it put right. Owning the lapse openly resets the standard for everyone and shows that challenging a manager on safety is welcome rather than risky.

questions.explanation: A leader's behaviour sets the working standard more strongly than any written rule, and teams copy the exceptions their leaders make. When a leader has visibly broken a norm, correcting it privately is not enough: the people who saw the lapse need to see it owned, or the unspoken rule remains that the standard is for others. Owning a lapse openly also makes it safer for anyone else to be challenged.
questions.mindset: Hold yourself to the standard you ask of the team, and own it openly when you slip.

questions.stem: Your team at a travel-booking platform agreed in its working agreement that pull requests are reviewed within one working day. Over the last three sprints one senior developer, Callum, has regularly left reviews for three or four days, and stories are stalling as a result. Two developers come to you privately and ask you, as delivery lead, to 'have a word with him'. Nobody has yet told Callum that anyone is unhappy. What should you do?

options.text: Speak to Callum privately, explain the impact the delayed reviews are having on flow, and ask him to commit to the agreed review time.
options.rationale: It solves this case by taking over a job that belongs to the team. Callum hears a peer complaint second-hand from his delivery lead, and the team learns to route every friction about its own agreement through you.

options.text: Encourage the two developers to raise it with Callum themselves, and offer to help them plan the conversation or facilitate it if they prefer.
options.rationale: The agreement is the team's, so holding each other to it is the team's job, and Callum deserves to hear it from the people affected first. Offering support builds the team's ability to do this without making you the enforcer.

options.text: Put review turnaround on the next retrospective agenda and show the team's review-time data, without naming anyone, so the group can address it.
options.rationale: Anonymised data about one person is a public reprimand in disguise when everyone knows who it is. The agreement itself is not in question; what is missing is a direct conversation that nobody has yet had with Callum.

options.text: Add an automated reminder to the team's board that flags any pull request waiting more than a day, so the delays become visible to everyone.
options.rationale: A tool answers a conversation problem. Callum may have reasons, such as being overloaded or unclear what is waiting on him, that a reminder will not surface, and the two developers' frustration stays unspoken.

questions.explanation: In a self-organising team the working agreement belongs to the team, and so does the job of holding each other to it. A leader who enforces it on the team's behalf turns a peer norm into a management rule and teaches the team to send every friction upwards. The leader's role is to build the team's ability to have the direct conversation, and to step in only when that has been tried and has not worked.
questions.mindset: Strengthen the team's ability to hold its own agreements rather than enforcing them for it.

questions.stem: You lead the €2.4 million installation of a new production line at an industrial bakery. A key supplier has slipped its delivery by two weeks, and the sponsor has just ended a heated call by calling the project 'a shambles' and demanding a recovery plan by Friday. You are angry at how the call went. Your weekly team meeting starts in ten minutes, and the team has not yet heard about the slip. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Hold the meeting, tell the team about the slip and the Friday deadline in factual terms, and start working through recovery options with them.
options.rationale: The team needs the facts and a part in the response, and the deadline leaves no slack for delay. Choosing a factual tone is the self-regulation the moment requires: the information passes on, the heat does not.

options.text: Postpone the meeting by a day so that you can settle, gather the supplier's revised dates, and then brief the team with a clearer picture.
options.rationale: Recognising your own state is right, but delay is the wrong response to it. A day lost out of a four-day window matters, the team may hear about the slip elsewhere first, and ten minutes is enough to decide what tone to take.

options.text: Hold the meeting and pass on the sponsor's comments as she made them, so the team understands how seriously the slip is being taken.
options.rationale: Transparency about substance is right; transmitting unfiltered anger is not. Relaying the sponsor's words hands the team your emotional load and invites defensiveness when what you need from them is clear thinking about recovery.

options.text: Hold the meeting as planned on its usual agenda, and work up the recovery plan with the two leads so the wider team is not unsettled.
options.rationale: Shielding the team turns into withholding from it. They will learn about the slip anyway, and the recovery plan loses the ideas of the people closest to the installation work.

questions.explanation: A leader under pressure from above has to separate the information from the emotion that came with it. The team needs the facts, the deadline and a part in the response; it does not need the leader's frustration or the sponsor's tone. Recognising your own state and choosing how to act on it is the skill, and that usually means deciding the tone of a conversation rather than delaying it or keeping the news back.
questions.mindset: Pass on the content of pressure from above, and absorb its heat yourself.

questions.stem: Your £38 million rail signalling upgrade has eight weeks of commissioning left. The team of fourteen engineers, half of them on fixed-term contracts, has gone quiet; output has fallen, and two engineers mention they are interviewing elsewhere. Nobody has told the team what happens to them after commissioning, and you have not raised it with anyone. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Talk with each engineer about what they want to do next, and take those wishes to their line managers and the resourcing team now.
options.rationale: Uncertainty about the future is what is draining effort, and the project manager can start reducing it immediately. Raising each person's wishes while there are still eight weeks to arrange something gives the next step a real chance of being in place.

options.text: Tell the team plainly what you know and do not yet know about post-project roles, and when you expect to be able to tell them more.
options.rationale: Partial certainty is better than silence, which people fill with the worst case. Being straight about what is unknown, and when that will change, lets the team commit to finishing instead of hedging.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to fund a completion bonus for engineers who stay until commissioning is signed off, to keep the team together to the end.
options.rationale: Money can hold people for eight weeks, but it does not touch the cause, which is not knowing what comes next. It also needs budget and approval the project manager does not hold, and it sets a precedent for future projects.

options.text: Hold off discussing next roles until commissioning is finished, so that the team's attention stays on the work still in front of it.
options.rationale: The silence is what is causing the drift. Postponing the conversation does not keep attention on the work; it leaves people to resolve their uncertainty on their own, including by leaving.

options.text: Agree to release any engineer early once they have secured their next role, so that goodwill is kept and nobody feels trapped by the project.
options.rationale: It trades away the commissioning capacity the project needs most, and an open-ended release promise can empty the team just before sign-off. Goodwill matters, but not at the cost of finishing the work.

questions.explanation: Toward the end of a project, team members' attention shifts to what comes next, and uncertainty about their future shows up as falling output long before anyone leaves. Leading the closing phase includes working actively on people's transitions and being honest about what is and is not known, because even partial certainty is what lets people commit to finishing. Waiting until the work is done to talk about what follows leaves the team to resolve its uncertainty alone.
questions.mindset: Treat the team's next step as part of the project's last one.

questions.stem: On a hybrid programme building an online grocer's fulfilment platform, you introduced a monthly 'save of the month' shout-out at the all-hands. Every winner so far has worked through the night to fix a live incident. Incidents have risen over the same period, and a monitoring improvement that has prevented several outages has never been mentioned. Nobody appears to be gaming the award deliberately. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Change what the shout-out celebrates: recognise the monitoring work and other prevention publicly, and explain to the team why the focus is shifting.
options.rationale: The award is the project manager's own lever, and redirecting it changes the signal at once. Explaining the shift makes the reason visible, so the team understands that preventing an outage is now valued at least as much as recovering from one.

options.text: Drop the shout-out altogether, on the basis that any award connected with live incidents will keep rewarding firefighting whatever criteria are written for it.
options.rationale: It discards a lever that works because of what it has been pointed at. The problem is what is being recognised, not that recognition exists, and removing it leaves prevention just as invisible as before.

options.text: Ask HR to design a formal recognition scheme for the programme, with written criteria that weigh incident response, prevention and quality work.
options.rationale: It escalates something already within the project manager's gift and replaces a quick adjustment with a slow, formal process. Meanwhile the existing award keeps sending the same signal every month.

options.text: Keep the shout-out as it is and add a second monthly award for prevention, so the incident responders do not feel their effort is being devalued.
options.rationale: Kind to the responders, but it keeps a headline award for heroics, so the strongest signal still points at overnight recovery. Two awards with one for firefighting tells the team both are equal when the evidence says one is feeding the other.

questions.explanation: What a leader recognises tells the team what is valued, and recognition that celebrates heroic recovery quietly rewards the conditions that make heroics necessary. Prevention is invisible by nature, because an outage that did not happen leaves nothing to applaud, so a leader has to make it visible deliberately. Recognition is one of the few levers a project manager fully controls, and adjusting it is usually quicker and more effective than creating a formal scheme.
questions.mindset: Recognise the work you want more of, especially the work that leaves nothing dramatic behind.

questions.stem: Your team builds a booking app for a chain of veterinary practices. Four developers work in the office and three work remotely most days. In the last month two design decisions were settled in conversations at the office whiteboard, and the remote developers found out only when their code conflicted with them. One of them says she now feels more like a contractor than a member of the team. What should you do?

options.text: Ask the remote developers to come into the office on two set days a week so that design discussions happen when everyone is present.
options.rationale: It imposes a working pattern that may be beyond your authority to set, and corridor conversations will still happen on the other three days. It relocates the people rather than changing where decisions are made.

options.text: Move all team meetings to video, with every member joining from their own laptop even when in the office, so that everyone takes part on equal terms.
options.rationale: Good practice for meetings, but neither decision was made in a meeting. The whiteboard conversations that caused the conflict would carry on exactly as before.

options.text: Agree with the team that design decisions are made or confirmed in the shared channel, where remote members can comment before they take effect.
options.rationale: The problem is an invisible decision channel, not the location of the people. A team norm about where decisions become real lets informal conversations keep happening while making sure everyone can see and shape the outcome.

options.text: Reopen the two design decisions with the whole team, so that the remote developers can contribute and the conflicting code is resolved properly.
options.rationale: It repairs the two instances at the cost of rework and leaves the pattern that produced them untouched. The next whiteboard decision will exclude the remote developers in the same way.

questions.explanation: In a team split between office and remote work, informal conversations near the office become a hidden decision channel, and remote members are excluded without anyone intending it. The remedy is a team norm about where decisions become real, somewhere everyone can see and contribute, rather than trying to equalise physical presence or repairing each case after the fact. Inclusion in a distributed team is designed into how decisions are made, not left to goodwill.
questions.mindset: Make the place where decisions happen one that every team member can reach.

questions.stem: You are forming the project team for a regional airport's terminal refurbishment and drafting its team charter. Earlier projects at the airport suffered from the recurring frictions below. Match each friction to the charter element that would prevent it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Engineers received messages late in the evening and felt expected to reply before the next morning's site meeting.
Two discipline leads disagreed over a ceiling-void layout for three weeks because nobody knew how such a dispute was to be settled.
Drawings and markups were kept in email, a shared drive and two separate tools, so people often worked from superseded versions.

options.text: Communication norms, including expected response times and hours of availability
options.rationale: The friction came from an unstated expectation about when replies were due. Writing down response times and availability hours removes the guesswork and the pressure that came with it.

options.text: A conflict-resolution process naming how disagreements are escalated and who decides if the leads cannot agree
options.rationale: Disagreement between specialists is normal; three weeks of it is a missing process. A known route and a named decider let a dispute end on merit without anyone having to back down publicly.

options.text: Agreed tools and information-handling rules naming the single location for current documents
options.rationale: Working from superseded drawings is a consequence of having several places that might hold the truth. Agreeing one location for current documents is a working rule the team can check itself against.

options.text: A resource calendar showing each team member's planned working days and leave
options.rationale: Not used. A resource calendar plans when people are available to work. It is tempting for the late-evening messages because it mentions availability, but that friction was about expectations of response, which a calendar does not set.

questions.explanation: A team charter sets expectations before friction appears, and each element exists to settle a question teams otherwise argue about repeatedly: how and when we communicate, how disagreements are resolved, where the working information lives. Drafting it from known past frictions turns lessons from earlier projects into agreements the new team has made for itself. A charter that states values without these working rules rarely changes behaviour.
questions.mindset: Settle how the team will work before the first disagreement makes it urgent.

questions.stem: You lead a hybrid team at an engineering consultancy designing a flood-defence scheme. Every milestone so far has been celebrated with Friday-evening drinks at a nearby pub. Ines, a hydrologist, mentions in passing that she has missed every one because she collects her children at 17:30, and another colleague does not drink and tends to leave after a few minutes. Both say the evenings are where much of the team's informal planning happens. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Keep the Friday drinks, which most of the team enjoys, and make sure soft drinks and food are ordered so that everyone feels welcome there.
options.rationale: It answers part of one colleague's situation and none of the other's. The timing still excludes anyone with caring responsibilities, and the informal planning still happens where some of the team cannot be.

options.text: Continue the Friday drinks, and post a short summary of any planning ideas raised there to the team channel on Monday morning.
options.rationale: It patches the information gap but keeps a two-tier team: those who shape ideas in person and those who read about them afterwards. Belonging is the issue as much as information.

options.text: Stop holding social events for the team, so that nobody is at a disadvantage and all project planning stays inside working meetings.
options.rationale: An overcorrection that removes something the team values. Celebrations build the relationships a team relies on; the problem is that this one suits only some people.

options.text: Vary the format and timing of celebrations, such as a team lunch in working hours, and ask the team for ideas on what would suit everyone.
options.rationale: Changing the format lets everyone take part, and asking the team avoids the leader guessing at what will suit people. Social time stays, but it stops depending on one habit that excludes some members.

questions.explanation: Team-building that depends on one time, place or habit includes the people it suits and quietly excludes others, often those with caring responsibilities, different beliefs or different health needs. When informal events also carry real work, exclusion from them becomes exclusion from the team. An inclusive leader adapts the format so that everyone can take part, and asks the team rather than guessing what will suit them.
questions.mindset: Design team rituals around who is on the team, not around who started them.

questions.stem: Two developers on your language-learning app team ask to move to a compressed week of four ten-hour days with Fridays off. Company policy allows this with the line manager's agreement, and you are their line manager. The team pairs on most stories and holds a daily stand-up. Some colleagues are worried about who will cover reviews and pairing on Fridays, while others say they might want the same pattern. What should you do?

options.text: Approve both requests, since policy allows them, and adjust the stand-up time and pairing rota yourself so that the team's Friday cover is arranged.
options.rationale: It decides the team's working arrangement for it. The colleagues' concerns go unheard, and with others likely to ask for the same, approving individuals one at a time builds a pattern nobody has designed.

options.text: Ask the whole team to work out how pairing, reviews and stand-ups would run under the new pattern, then agree a trial with a review date.
options.rationale: The people who will absorb the change can see the practical problems best and will work harder to make a plan of their own succeed. A trial with a review date keeps the decision reversible while ownership is shared.

options.text: Approve one request now and the other in three months, so that the effect on pairing can be judged before Friday cover is reduced any further.
options.rationale: Staggering is a reasonable instinct, but choosing which developer waits is arbitrary and likely to feel unfair. It also keeps the experiment in the manager's hands when the people affected are best placed to design it.

options.text: Decline both requests for now, explaining that pairing depends on shared working hours and that the team's way of working would be disrupted.
options.rationale: It assumes the arrangement cannot work without testing whether it can. Refusing flexibility that policy allows may cost you the people who asked, and the concern about pairing is one the team could probably solve.

questions.explanation: When a working-pattern request affects how a self-organising team collaborates, the people who will absorb the impact are best placed to design how it can work. The leader still holds the formal decision, but turning it into a team problem with a trial and a review date surfaces practical issues early and spreads ownership of making it work. Deciding alone, in either direction, leaves the team living with an arrangement it did not shape.
questions.mindset: Let the people who will live with a working arrangement design it, within the limits you hold.

questions.stem: Your sports-streaming team of five had worked smoothly for a year. Three developers joined a month ago. Since then stand-ups have doubled in length, the newcomers have questioned the team's definition of done and its branching strategy, and two long-standing members complain that settled matters keep being reopened. Velocity has fallen for two sprints. Which two actions should you take?

options.text: Run a session with the whole team of eight to revisit the working agreements and the definition of done, with the newcomers' challenges on the table.
options.rationale: An enlarged team is a new team, and agreements the newcomers had no part in are not yet theirs. Reopening them together lets their challenges be tested on merit and gives everyone ownership of whatever comes out.

options.text: Agree with the product owner a lower forecast for the next two sprints while the enlarged team settles into a new way of working.
options.rationale: A dip while a team re-forms is normal and predictable. Resetting expectations with the product owner removes pressure that would otherwise push the team to skip the work of re-forming.

options.text: Ask the long-standing members to walk the newcomers through the existing agreements and explain the reasons each one was adopted.
options.rationale: It treats the agreements as fixed rules to be learned rather than commitments the new team makes together. The newcomers may understand them better but will not own them, and some of their challenges may be right.

options.text: Settle the disputed points on branching and the definition of done yourself, so the team stops spending sprint time on reopened debates.
options.rationale: A directive shortcut ends the debate but takes ownership away from the team at exactly the moment it needs to rebuild it. Decisions imposed on a storming team tend to be reopened again later.

options.text: Split the team into two squads, one of the original members and one of the newcomers, until the newcomers have fully settled in.
options.rationale: It entrenches an in-group and an out-group and postpones the integration the team needs. Five people who already work well together do not teach three newcomers how to join them by working apart.

questions.explanation: Changing a team's membership creates a new team, and a group that had been performing commonly goes back through earlier stages of development, including a period of challenge and conflict. That is normal rather than a failure. The leader's job is to let the enlarged team rebuild its agreements together, so that newcomers own them as much as founders do, and to set expectations with stakeholders that performance will dip while it happens.
questions.mindset: When membership changes, expect to rebuild the team rather than just onboard new people.

questions.stem: You manage the design of a £60 million hospital wing for an architectural practice. Six architects each name layers, files and annotations in their own way. Last month the structural consultant's model failed to import two floors because layer names were inconsistent, costing a week of rework. When you propose a common standard, the two most experienced architects object that the practice's 80-page CAD manual would slow them down for no benefit. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Agree with the architects a short shared convention covering only what other disciplines import or read, and leave each person's internal working style alone.
options.rationale: The failure happened at the interface with another discipline, so that is where consistency earns its cost. Agreeing a minimal convention with the people who must use it gets their commitment and leaves them the freedom that does not harm anyone else.

options.text: Adopt the practice's CAD manual in full for this project, on the basis that one complete standard is easier to audit than a partial one agreed locally.
options.rationale: It treats the objection as resistance to be overruled rather than information. Imposing eighty pages of rules to solve a problem located at one interface spends the team's goodwill and time on conventions nobody downstream relies on.

options.text: Leave conventions to each architect and appoint a coordinator to check and correct every file against the consultants' needs before it is issued.
options.rationale: It protects autonomy by adding a permanent correction step that the architects never have to think about. The cost of inconsistency moves to one person, and the habit that caused the rework is left in place.

options.text: Ask the structural consultant to set out the conventions they need from your drawings, and instruct the architects to follow that specification from the next issue.
options.rationale: Closer, because it targets the interface, but it hands the design of the team's working rules to an outside party and then imposes them by instruction. The architects who objected have no part in the answer and less reason to keep to it.

questions.explanation: Standards and autonomy trade against each other, and the leader's job is to decide where consistency is worth its cost rather than choosing one wholesale. Consistency pays where other people depend on the output; inside someone's own work it mostly adds friction. Agreeing the boundary with the people who will work within it is what turns a rule into a team norm.
questions.mindset: Standardise where other people depend on the output, and leave freedom everywhere else.

questions.stem: During a sprint review for a housing association's tenant portal, a senior stakeholder interrupts a junior developer's demonstration to say, in front of fifteen people, that the bug she has just exposed is 'amateurish' and that he expects better. The developer falls silent. The bug is real but minor, and the team had already logged it in the backlog. As delivery lead, what should you do?

options.text: Let the demonstration continue so as not to embarrass anyone further, then speak privately to the stakeholder afterwards about how his comment landed.
options.rationale: Speaking to him privately is worth doing, but letting the moment pass in public tells the developer and everyone watching that this treatment is acceptable. Whatever is said later, the room only saw silence.

options.text: Ask the developer to explain the cause of the bug and the planned fix, so the stakeholder can see that the team has it under control.
options.rationale: It answers the substance but leaves a junior colleague to defend herself in front of the person who has just criticised her. Putting her back on the spot is the opposite of the cover she needs at that moment.
