options.text: Step in at once to say the defect belongs to the team and is already in the backlog, then move the review on and raise his tone with him afterwards.
options.rationale: Intervening in the moment shows the team that a public attack on one member will be met by the leader, and reframing the bug as the team's removes the personal target. The conversation about his conduct still happens, privately and later.

options.text: Suggest a short break so that tempers can cool, check on the developer while it lasts, and resume the review with the next item on the agenda.
options.rationale: A break defuses the room but avoids the issue. Nothing is said about the comment, nobody hears that the bug is already the team's, and the stakeholder learns that this behaviour simply pauses the meeting.

questions.explanation: When a team member is attacked in public, the leader's response has to happen in the same place and at the same time, because everyone watching is learning what is tolerated. Taking collective ownership of the problem removes the individual target, and the separate conversation about conduct belongs in private afterwards. Psychological safety is built in these moments far more than in any statement of values.
questions.mindset: Protect the team in the room where it was exposed, and correct the behaviour in private later.

questions.stem: You lead a programme replacing an airline's crew-rostering system: a stage-gated vendor integration alongside two in-house scrum teams. In the quarterly anonymous engagement survey, agreement with 'my views are listened to' has fallen from 78% to 41% in one quarter, while every other score is steady and delivery is on track. HR offers to run a facilitated listening-skills workshop for your team leads. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Accept HR's offer and book the listening-skills workshop for the team leads promptly, since the score points directly at how the team's views are heard and acted on.
options.rationale: It accepts the first explanation offered. A sharp fall in one quarter suggests something changed, such as a decision made over the team's heads, and a skills course for leads will not touch that if it is the cause.

options.text: Share the result openly with both teams, and run a session with an anonymous way to contribute so they can say what changed before you choose a response.
options.rationale: Showing the team the result proves the survey was read, and asking them what changed finds the cause before a remedy is picked. An anonymous channel keeps faith with the way the concern was first raised.

options.text: Hold one-to-one conversations with each team member over the next fortnight to find out who feels unheard and what lies behind it.
options.rationale: The instinct to ask is right, but the survey was anonymous, and asking each person individually reads as looking for who answered. People who feel unheard are the least likely to say so face to face with the leader.

options.text: Wait for next quarter's survey to confirm whether the fall persists before acting, since delivery is on track and a single result can be noise.
options.rationale: A drop of more than thirty points on one question while others hold steady is a signal, not noise. Waiting three months tells the team that the survey goes nowhere, which will itself depress the next result.

questions.explanation: A team measure that moves sharply tells you something changed, not what changed, and the first remedy on offer is usually a guess at the cause. The leader's first move is to take the result back to the people who produced it, in a way that respects how they chose to say it, and let them explain it. Acting on a diagnosis the team never gave risks solving the wrong problem while showing them they were not heard a second time.
questions.mindset: Ask the team what a signal means before deciding what to do about it.

questions.stem: On a design-and-build contract for a €45 million water treatment works, the design and site teams report to different directors in your firm. Designers are bonused on issuing drawings by milestone dates; site engineers are bonused on avoiding rework. Site engineers now reject drawings over minor queries, and designers issue early to hit dates. The sponsor calls it a personality clash and asks you to arrange a facilitated team-building day. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Arrange the team-building day as asked, but design it around the interface between the teams so that the tension over targets can be discussed openly.
options.rationale: The most tempting answer, because it honours the sponsor's request and surfaces the real issue. But neither team can change its own bonus terms, so an open discussion ends in shared frustration while both targets keep pulling as before.

options.text: Introduce a joint readiness review at which designers and site engineers agree acceptance criteria before each drawing issue, to cut both early issues and needless rejections.
options.rationale: A sound process step that could reduce the friction for a while. Yet each side remains paid for the behaviour the review is meant to stop, so the review itself becomes the place where dates and rejections are fought over.

options.text: Ask each director to brief their own staff that cooperation across the interface is expected, and that the current behaviour is harming the project.
options.rationale: It routes the issue to the people with authority over each team, which is half right. But it asks staff to act against the targets those same directors set, and an instruction to cooperate rarely outweighs a bonus.

options.text: Explain to the sponsor that the two bonus targets pull against each other, and propose to both directors a shared project measure such as drawings accepted first time.
options.rationale: The behaviour is what the incentives reward, so it will survive any amount of goodwill. Naming the structural cause to the sponsor and proposing a measure both teams win or lose together addresses the reason the friction exists.

questions.explanation: When two groups behave badly towards each other in a consistent, predictable way, look at what each is measured and rewarded on before concluding that the problem is personal. Team-building, process fixes and instructions to cooperate all treat the symptom while the incentive keeps producing it. A leader who can see a structural cause has to name it to the people who own the structure, even when they have already chosen a different explanation.
questions.mindset: Before blaming personalities, check what each side is being rewarded for.

questions.stem: Your team maintains a bank's mortgage-application service. For four sprints nobody except two senior developers has picked up stories that touch the affordability-calculation module, and both are now visibly tired and working late. The rest of the team picks up everything else readily. At today's sprint planning the module's stories again sat unclaimed until the two seniors took them. What should you do?

options.text: Pair each senior developer with a colleague on the module's stories next sprint, so that knowledge of the calculation spreads across the wider team and the load is shared.
options.rationale: The strongest alternative, and right if the cause is a knowledge gap. But the others take on unfamiliar work elsewhere readily, which hints at something else, such as fear of blame for errors in a regulated calculation, and pairing will not remove that.

options.text: Agree with the team that the module's stories rotate through every developer in turn, with the two seniors available to review the changes.
options.rationale: Rotation spreads the load by rule, but it forces people into work they have been avoiding without learning why. If the reason is something like harsh review or blame, rotation makes everyone anxious rather than solving it.

options.text: Raise the pattern with the team at the retrospective and ask what makes those stories unattractive before agreeing any change to how they are shared.
options.rationale: Consistent avoidance by capable people has a reason, and the team knows it. Finding it first means the eventual remedy, whether pairing, review changes or test support, fits the actual cause rather than the most likely-sounding one.

options.text: Ask the two senior developers to stop taking module stories for one sprint, so that others have to take them on and learn the module by doing.
options.rationale: It relieves the two seniors but turns the module into a test of nerve for the rest, and the stories may simply stay unclaimed with the sprint goal at risk. It acts on the symptom before anyone knows the cause.

questions.explanation: When a self-organising team consistently avoids one kind of work, the avoidance is information: something about that work, such as risk, blame, poor tooling or a difficult reviewer, makes it costly to pick up. Remedies such as pairing or rotation each assume a particular cause, so choosing one before finding out is a guess. Asking the team names the cause and gives them ownership of the fix.
questions.mindset: Treat work a capable team avoids as a question to ask, not a rota to impose.

questions.stem: You manage the design of a road bridge for a county council. A structural engineer by background, you have been quietly rechecking and correcting two junior engineers' load calculations each evening before they go to the independent checker. Over three months their errors have increased rather than fallen, and one remarked that 'it gets fixed anyway'. You are now working most evenings. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Stop correcting their calculations yourself, and return any error you notice to the engineer concerned to fix, with an explanation of what went wrong.
options.rationale: The silent safety net is what has removed the consequence of the errors, as the 'gets fixed anyway' remark shows. Returning the work with an explanation makes the engineers responsible for it and turns each error into learning.

options.text: Agree with the junior engineers and the checker the standard a calculation must meet before submission, and make each engineer accountable for meeting it.
options.rationale: An explicit, shared standard replaces your private judgement with an expectation the engineers can check themselves against. Accountability for meeting it is what the evening corrections had quietly taken away.

options.text: Arrange a formal structural-analysis course for the two junior engineers, so that their technical knowledge catches up with what the project demands.
options.rationale: It assumes a skills gap, but the errors grew while you were correcting them, which points to lost ownership rather than lost knowledge. A course on top of an unchanged safety net leaves the incentive to be careless in place.

options.text: Ask the engineering manager to replace one of the juniors with a more experienced engineer, to bring the error rate down before the next design stage.
options.rationale: It blames the people for a pattern the project manager created. A more experienced engineer may make fewer errors, but the remaining junior still works under the same safety net, and the team loses the chance to develop.

options.text: Continue checking for now, but keep a log of each correction you make so you can discuss the pattern with each engineer at their next appraisal.
options.rationale: Recording the pattern is useful, but it keeps the safety net in place for months and saves the feedback for a formal review. Feedback delayed to an appraisal arrives long after it could have changed anything.

questions.explanation: A leader who quietly fixes the team's work removes the feedback that would have improved it, and the team adjusts its effort to the safety net. Developing people means returning their work to them with an explanation and setting an explicit standard they own, even when doing it yourself is faster. The leader's technical skill is better spent on coaching than on correcting.
questions.mindset: If you keep catching the team's mistakes, ask whether your catching is why they keep making them.

questions.stem: You lead a hybrid programme for a pharmaceutical distributor, with team members in Manchester, Pune and Seoul. Match each situation to the leadership response that best addresses it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Engineers in Seoul rarely raise objections in design reviews chaired by the chief architect, but send detailed concerns by email afterwards.
A developer in Pune answers 'that may be difficult' when asked about dates, and it later emerges this meant the date could not be met.
A major release has been scheduled for the week of Diwali, when most of the Pune team expects to be on leave.

options.text: Collect written views before each review and open the meeting with them, so objections do not depend on challenging a senior figure aloud
options.rationale: The concerns exist and are well-formed; what holds them back is the setting. Bringing written input into the meeting first lets the objections shape the decision without anyone having to contradict the chief architect in public.

options.text: Agree an explicit, shared way of flagging that a date is at risk, so that a 'no' does not depend on how directly someone speaks
options.rationale: Indirect refusal is a normal way of saying no in many cultures. A shared status convention makes the message unambiguous without asking anyone to abandon their own manner of speaking.

options.text: Keep a shared calendar of each location's public holidays and festivals, and check it whenever release dates are set
options.rationale: The clash came from one location's calendar being invisible to the people planning. Making every location's holidays part of release planning prevents it rather than relying on someone noticing in time.

options.text: Raise it privately with the individuals concerned and ask them to be more direct and open in future team meetings
options.rationale: Not used. It is tempting for the first two situations, but it treats a cultural difference as a personal shortcoming and asks people to change their behaviour instead of changing the process so their views reach the team.

questions.explanation: In a team that spans cultures, much of what goes wrong comes from norms that one part of the team treats as obvious and the rest cannot see: how disagreement is expressed, how refusal is phrased, which days matter. The leader's job is to make those norms explicit and build them into how the team works, rather than asking individuals to adopt the dominant group's style. Designing the process around the differences lets everyone's view reach the team.
questions.mindset: Change the process so differences can be heard, rather than asking people to sound the same.

questions.stem: You are delivery lead for a team building a ticketing platform for a football club. Complete each sentence with the way of making the decision that fits the situation. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: The team must decide how out-of-hours on-call duty will be shared over the coming season, and every member will live with the result. It should be decided by
Ticket sales have failed during a live on-sale, and two engineers are proposing different rollbacks while thousands of fans wait. It should be decided by
The team needs an indexing approach for the seat-availability database, and only one engineer has the depth to judge the options. It should be decided by

options.text: the whole team, working towards an outcome every member can support
options.rationale: On-call duty touches everyone's evenings and weekends, and it only works if people honour it when it is inconvenient. Commitment of that kind comes from an outcome each person has accepted, which justifies the extra time consensus takes.

options.text: the named incident lead, deciding at once and reviewing the call afterwards
options.rationale: In a live failure the cost of delay outweighs the cost of a less-than-perfect choice. A single named decider acts now, and the review afterwards is where the team learns whether the call was right.

options.text: the engineer with the expertise, after hearing the others' concerns, by an agreed date
options.rationale: Where judgement depends on knowledge only one person has, a group decision dilutes it. Hearing the others' concerns first and fixing a date keeps the decision informed and timely without pretending everyone can weigh it equally.

options.text: a majority vote of the team at the next planning session
options.rationale: Not used. A vote is quick and looks fair, but here it is too slow for the outage, ignores the expertise the database choice needs, and leaves a dissenting minority carrying on-call duty they never accepted.

questions.explanation: How a decision is made should follow from what the decision needs: urgency calls for a single named decider, deep specialist knowledge for the expert with input from others, and outcomes that depend on everyone's commitment for consensus. Using one method for everything either slows urgent calls or imposes decisions that need buy-in. A leader's job is to make the method explicit before the decision, so the team knows how it will be made.
questions.mindset: Choose how a decision is made according to what the decision needs, before making it.

questions.stem: Your five-engineer team on a gas network upgrade gains two new engineers next month. Each newcomer is expected to deliver 25%, 50% and 75% of a full engineer's output in months 1, 2 and 3. Each is assigned a mentor from the existing team, who loses 30%, 20% and 10% of their own output over the same three months. Work out the effect on team output in full-time-equivalent (FTE) terms.

blanks.label: Net change in team output in month 1, in FTE (use a minus sign for a fall)
blanks.rationale: Newcomers add 2 × 0.25 = 0.5 FTE; mentors lose 2 × 0.30 = 0.6 FTE. Net change is 0.5 − 0.6 = −0.1 FTE, so in the first month the team produces slightly less than it did before the newcomers arrived.

blanks.label: Number of the first month in which net team output is higher than before the newcomers arrived
blanks.rationale: Month 2: newcomers add 2 × 0.50 = 1.0 FTE and mentors lose 2 × 0.20 = 0.4 FTE, a net gain of 0.6 FTE. Month 1 was −0.1, so month 2 is the first month with a net gain.

blanks.label: Net extra output over months 1 to 3 combined, in FTE-months
blanks.rationale: Newcomers contribute 2 × (0.25 + 0.50 + 0.75) = 3.0 FTE-months; mentoring costs 2 × (0.30 + 0.20 + 0.10) = 1.2 FTE-months. The net gain is 3.0 − 1.2 = 1.8 FTE-months, well short of the 6 FTE-months two full engineers would add.

questions.explanation: Adding people to a team reduces its output before it increases it, because newcomers start below full productivity and the people who bring them up to speed lose time of their own. A leader planning growth should model both effects, set stakeholders' expectations for the early dip, and protect the mentoring time rather than treating it as lost capacity. Headcount and capacity are different numbers until onboarding is complete.
questions.mindset: Count the cost of bringing people up to speed before counting what they will add.

questions.stem: The diagram maps a fortnight of design decisions on your hybrid team building a ferry operator's booking system. Each box shows a person, how many decisions waited on them, and the average wait. The team says decisions are too slow. Select the person whose part in the flow is adding the most total delay and should be addressed first.

graphic.title: Decision flow map: who the team waited on, with decision counts and average waits
graphic.caption: Select a person. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between them, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Ana, tech lead — 14 decisions, average wait 3 hours
regions.rationale: Ana handles the most decisions, which makes her look like the bottleneck, but at three hours each her total delay is under two working days. Volume through a person is not the same as delay.

regions.label: You, project manager — 11 decisions, average wait 2.5 days
regions.rationale: Eleven decisions at two and a half days each is about 27 days of waiting, far more than anyone else. It is also the delay you can remove most directly, by delegating decisions or setting a response time for yourself.

regions.label: Tom, product owner — 6 decisions, average wait 1 day
regions.rationale: Six days of total waiting is noticeable but well below the largest source. Starting here would improve the flow a little while the main delay continued.

regions.label: Lena, architect — 4 decisions, average wait 4 hours
regions.rationale: Four decisions at four hours each adds up to about two working days. Lena responds quickly and handles few decisions, so she contributes little of the delay.

regions.label: Kofi, vendor liaison — 3 decisions, average wait 5 days
regions.rationale: The longest average wait catches the eye, but three decisions at five days is about 15 days in total, roughly half the largest source. Reading the average alone, without the count, leads here.

questions.explanation: To find where a team loses time, multiply how often work waits on someone by how long it waits; neither the count nor the average alone identifies the bottleneck. Leaders are often part of the delay themselves, because decisions flow to them by habit and their attention is spread thinly. The quickest improvement is frequently one within the leader's own control: delegating decisions or committing to a response time.
questions.mindset: Look for the bottleneck in your own diary before looking for it in the team.
